newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: GROLSCH 1996 NET SEEN HIGHER ON EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: GROLSCH 1996 NET SEEN HIGHER ON EXPORTS.

text.p: Consolidation of its Polish interests and higher exports are likely to have helped Dutch brewer Grolsch lift 1996 profit by an average of seven percent, analysts said.
Profit forecasts of Wednesday's results range from 59.2 to 66.9 million guilders, up from 59 million net profit in 1995.

"Organic growth is estimated in the region of seven percent, mainly driven by higher exports and sales of beer under licence, notably notably in the UK and Poland and higher exports of the Amsterdam Navigator brand to Russia," ABN AMRO analyst David Kerstens said.
Analysts said the growth in exports and the consolidation of Polish activities were likely to have more than compensated for the impact of last year's poor European summer on consumption.
Darrell Duthie, analyst at MeesPierson, said he did not expect Grolsch Dutch beer sales to have suffered enormously from last year's mild summer.
"In the Netherlands, some 60 percent of Grolsch sales are destined for home consumption, which is less sensitive to sunny weather than the on-trade business," he said.
Gerard Rijk, analyst at ING Barings, only partially agreed, as home consumption includes barbecueing.
Duthie said increased marketing efforts were likely to have resulted in a slight rise in Grolsch' market share in the Netherlands.

Analysts agreed that Grolsch' sales in the rest of Europe, notably in Poland, were likely to have been pressured by the poor weather, but less than rival Dutch brewer Heineken's due to their different geographical spreads.
"Grolsch also improved margins in Poland. It's interesting to hear more about their prospects on the somewhat longer term in that country," Duthie said.

Analysts were positive on the long-term prospects of the distribution agreement between Grolsch and Canada's Seagram signed last year, but added that 1996 U.S. sales would be down on 1995 due to the start-up of new distribution contracts.

"It fits perfectly with the increasing wish for tasty beer in the U.S., turning import beers into a growing market segment. But beer distribution is a profession on its own, and we'll have to wait and see if Seagram - originally a soft-drinks distributor - can do the job," said ING's Rijk.
"Grolsch might give a first impression on how things fare with the U.S. distribution," said Duthie.
Grolsch said in September last year it expected its 1996 net profit to be above that of 1995.
